subtype: Approach: divergent brainstorming of problems seen daily [Thinking]
passage: The engineering college outside Dharwad had two hostels, one mess and endless complaints. For a week, Rashmi carried a small notebook everywhere and wrote down every irritation she heard, with a tally beside it. The mess sambar being watery: nine. The one washing machine on each floor always broken or full: twenty-two. The college bus leaving early: six. No stationery shop nearby: four. On Sunday she showed Vaibhav the pages at the tea stall near the gate. "Laundry," he said at once. "Even I've complained about that." Rashmi nodded. "The mess bothers me more, honestly. But people mention laundry more than twice as often as anything else." She circled it. "That's what they'll care about. Not what I care about." Vaibhav looked at her. "So we're doing laundry?" "We're testing laundry," she said.

qa.q: How many times did people mention the washing machines?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.a: Rashmi is a little torn, bothered more by the mess personally, but convinced to follow what others complain about most.

subtype: Approach: talking to twenty potential users first [Action]
passage: In the hostel of the agricultural university in Palampur, Sabina spent two evenings knocking on doors with a notepad and a packet of biscuits. Her friend Maria came along to take notes. Twenty rooms, the same questions: How do you get your clothes washed now? What do you pay? What annoys you about it? Sabina didn't mention the laundry app the two of them had sketched. By the twentieth room, the pattern was clear. Most students washed by hand or used the washerwoman from the nearby village, who charged by the bucket. What annoyed them wasn't booking. It was the cost and the time in exam weeks, when nobody could wash. "Nobody said app once," Maria said, looking at the notes. Sabina laughed, a little embarrassed. "Then the app isn't the product. A cheap exam-week wash might be."

subtype: Approach: minimum viable version with a manual service [Action]
passage: In our third year, Arnab and I were sure the hostel needed a laundry app. I'm Lalit. We'd even sketched the screens. Then a senior asked us, "Has anyone paid you yet?" Nobody had. So instead of coding for three months, we made a chat group for one hostel block, Block C, and posted: "Laundry pickup Tuesday and Friday, 12 rupees a piece, washed and folded by the next evening." We collected the bags ourselves from the corridor, carried them to the laundromat near the gate on a borrowed cycle, and wrote every order in a notebook. For two weeks we did it all by hand. Twenty-three people ordered. Nine ordered twice. My shoulders ached from the bags. Looking back, those two weeks taught us more than any app would have: people would pay, but mostly just before exams.

qa.q: How many people ordered in two weeks?
qa.a: Twenty-three people ordered.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel during the two weeks?
qa.a: Lalit felt tired, with aching shoulders, but encouraged as real orders came in.

qa.q: What else could the pair try after the two weeks?
qa.a: They could run the same manual service in a second block or in exam weeks to see if demand holds, before building any app.

qa.q: How might the Block C residents see the service?
qa.a: Residents get cheap, easy laundry, and by ordering they show the founders whether people will really pay.

grounding: Shows founders running a manual laundry pickup for one hostel block through a chat group for two weeks, instead of coding an app, to see if anyone pays.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Block A, end of February.
For the past two weeks, Tanuja and Ishita from third year have run a laundry pickup service for this block by hand. They asked my permission first and posted the details on the block's chat group: pickup on Monday and Thursday evenings, 15 rupees a piece, returned in two days. No app, just a notebook and a list on the notice board.
I watched them drag bags down the stairs twice a week and fold clothes in the common room. Some residents were doubtful at first. By the second week the list had thirty-one names, and several students asked if it would continue during exams.
Tanuja told me they want to build an app, but wanted proof first that people would pay. I thought that was sensible.
Next step: they have asked to use the common room on Thursday evenings next month. I've agreed.

qa.a: 15 rupees a piece.

qa.a: Tanuja felt cautious about building an app too soon and wanted proof that people would pay before investing in one.

subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
passage:
September. Uday's idea arrived at 2 am: a campus app for renting out textbooks from seniors to juniors. At breakfast, four friends called it genius. Devika asked quietly, "Do juniors actually want old books, or do they just photocopy?" Uday waved it away. "Everyone needs books."
October. Uday spent most of his summer internship savings on a designer's logo and a polished website with a bookshelf animation. He didn't message a single junior outside his friend group.
November. Launch week. He posted in every college group. Eighty-three visits, zero rentals. One junior replied: "We just photocopy the important chapters, bhaiya." Uday read it three times. Then he opened his notes and found Devika's question from September, which he had typed out and never answered.

qa.a: A campus app for renting out textbooks from seniors to juniors.

qa.q: How did Uday feel reading the junior's reply?
qa.a: Uday was stunned and deflated, reading it three times as he realised Devika's early doubt had been right.

subtype: Approach: pre-mortem on the venture [Thinking]
passage: Mehak, you're starting a business in college? Good. Let me tell you what we did, back when I was twenty and ran a cycle-repair service on our campus with two friends, Farhan and Leela. Before we spent a rupee, Farhan made us do something strange. "Imagine it's one year from today and we've shut down. Why?" We sat on the hostel roof and listed it. One: exams, because all three of us would vanish in April. Two: a cofounder leaving. "Saurabh, that's you," Farhan said, "for an internship," and I had to admit it. Three: nobody coming back after the first repair. So we made a rule for each. We'd close in exam weeks and announce it early. Anyone leaving would give a month's notice and train someone. Every customer got a free check-up card for the next visit. We ran for three years, Mehak. We didn't shut down. We graduated.

qa.q: What three reasons for failure did they list?
qa.a: Exams, a cofounder leaving, and nobody coming back after the first repair.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when Farhan named the likely leaver?
qa.a: Saurabh seems a little sheepish but honest, having to admit an internship might pull Saurabh away first.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Making a rule for each imagined failure, like closing in exam weeks and giving check-up cards, because it turned vague fears into plans.

qa.q: How did Farhan see the need for the exercise?
qa.a: Farhan pushed for it before any money was spent, seeing that imagining failure early was the cheapest way to prevent it.

grounding: Shows founders imagining their venture failing after a year, listing exams, a cofounder leaving and no repeat customers, and setting a rule for each.

passage: Aditi, you asked how our tiffin pilot went. Honestly? We missed. I'm Saurabh, and I'll give you the numbers, because we promised ourselves we would. The goal for October was thirty repeat orders: people who ordered once and came back. We didn't count first orders, because friends order once to be nice. We kept a sheet, and every Sunday we counted, no rounding up. Week one: four. Week two: six. Week three: five. Week four: four. Nineteen. Not thirty. For about an hour I sulked. Then we looked at who came back. Almost all were students in the far hostel, where the mess is terrible. Nobody from the near hostel came back at all. So the target wasn't an insult. It told us where the real customers are. November's pilot: only the far hostel, same target.

qa.a: Nineteen. Not thirty.

subtype: Approach: rigid persistence despite weak signals [Pitfall]
passage: Six months into his campus bike-rental app, Tenzin had eleven regular users out of three thousand students. His cofounder Anand showed him the numbers in the hostel mess. "Maybe we should change something. Or pause." Tenzin shook his head. "Quitting is what failures do." Instead he added features: a leaderboard, bike reviews, a referral bonus. Each took weeks of coding at night. His mid-semester marks dropped in two subjects, and his savings from summer work thinned with every server bill. Then came the complication: the college announced its own free cycle scheme for the new semester. Anand pleaded, "Can we at least talk to the eleven users and ask why they stay?" Tenzin stared at the announcement on his phone. "We just need one more feature." That night he started coding a chat function, with an exam the next morning.

qa.a: Eleven regular users out of three thousand students.

subtype: Approach: adaptive replanning and pivot [Revision]
passage: In the campus incubator's small meeting room, Sabina spread three months of order sheets across the table. Their service had started as "anything delivered to your hostel room": snacks, stationery, medicines, printouts. Pema, her cofounder, had highlighted every printout order in yellow. The pages were mostly yellow in two places: the weeks before mid-terms and the weeks before finals. "Snacks, fourteen orders in three months," Pema said. "Printouts, two hundred and six." Sabina tapped the yellow. "People don't need us to deliver everything. They need notes printed at midnight before an exam." Their mentor, listening from the corner, raised an eyebrow. "So what changes?" Sabina took a breath. "We drop snacks and medicines. We become notes and printing only, and we stay open till 2 am in exam weeks." The next exam season, orders tripled.

qa.q: How many printout orders were there in three months?
qa.a: Two hundred and six.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel on seeing the yellow pages?
qa.a: Sabina felt a spark of realisation and excitement, seeing that printouts were what people truly needed.

qa.a: They could offer binding or a pickup point near the library, and keep checking the data each exam season.

qa.q: How might students see the change?
qa.a: Students get a reliable way to print notes late before exams, which is exactly the need they were already showing.

grounding: Shows founders noticing customers mostly use the service for exam-week printouts, narrowing it to notes and printing, and seeing orders grow.

subtype: Approach: adaptive replanning and pivot [Revision]

Subject: I think we should change what we are
Zubin,
I went through all 312 orders from August to November last night. Here's what I found.
We started as a general errand service for the hostels. But 71% of our orders were printouts, and almost all of them came in the ten days before exams. Grocery runs: 18 orders. Courier pickups: 9. The rest barely exist.
So the customers have already told us what we are. We just haven't listened.
My proposal: from December, we stop general errands and only print and deliver notes. We tie up with the print shop by the gate, take orders on a simple form, and deliver to rooms twice a night during exam weeks.
I know you liked the do-everything idea. So did I. But the numbers aren't close.
Can we talk tomorrow after the lab?
Suraj

subtype: Approach: seeking a mentor and campus incubator advice [Action]
passage: Wasim and Asif took the early bus from their college in Bijnor to the district incubation centre, carrying a folder and a lot of hope. Their idea was a service that collects farmers' soil samples and gets them tested at the city lab. The mentor, a retired bank officer who now helped young founders, listened to their pitch for ten minutes. Then he asked, "How many farmers have paid you so far?" Asif looked at Wasim. "None yet, sir. We wanted to find an investor first." The mentor smiled kindly. "Investors will ask the same question I just did." He walked them through what they'd need: registering properly before handling regular payments, working out what each sample really costs, bus fares included, and running a paid pilot in two or three villages first. On the bus home, Wasim wrote "Paid pilot: Haldaur, 20 farmers" at the top of the folder.

qa.q: What was their idea?
qa.a: A service that collects farmers' soil samples and gets them tested at the city lab.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt answering none yet?
qa.a: Asif probably felt a little embarrassed and deflated, glancing at Wasim before admitting no farmer had paid.

qa.q: What else could they prepare before the pilot?
qa.a: They could list every cost per sample and agree a fair price with the first farmers, so the pilot tests whether it truly works.

qa.q: How might the farmers in Haldaur see the pilot?
qa.a: The farmers would get soil tested without travelling to the city, and their willingness to pay will show whether the idea is worth building.

grounding: Illustrates founders seeking a mentor's advice at an incubator, learning about registration and costs, and seeing they need paid pilots before investors.
